title: Engineering Practices
description: Engineers identify problems and design solutions. They test, improve, and compare designs. Science knowledge about forces, materials, and the environment helps engineers solve real problems.

exercises.question: What is the FIRST step in the engineering design process?
choices: build the solution
test the solution
identify the problem
share the results
exercises.exp: Engineers start by clearly identifying the problem they need to solve — you cannot design a solution without knowing the problem!

exercises.question: After building a solution, engineers always ___.
choices: throw it away and start over
test it to see if it works and then improve it
sell it immediately
keep it secret
exercises.exp: Testing and improving is key to engineering. If the first design does not work perfectly, you redesign and try again!

exercises.question: A coastal town is losing beach because of EROSION. Which solution is BEST?
choices: remove all the sand
plant native grasses and install seawalls to stabilise the shoreline
dig deeper into the beach
do nothing and wait
exercises.exp: Native grasses have deep roots that hold soil. Seawalls block wave erosion — two strategies that work together!

exercises.question: Engineers are designing a FLOOD barrier for a town near a river. What is MOST important?
choices: the barrier looks beautiful
the barrier can hold back large amounts of water safely
the barrier is made of wood
the barrier is very small
exercises.exp: A flood barrier must safely hold back large volumes of water — that is the whole purpose of the design!

exercises.question: Why do engineers use MAGNETS to solve problems?
choices: magnets are very colourful
magnets can attract and repel objects without touching them
magnets are cheap to make
magnets only work in science class
exercises.exp: Magnets can move metallic objects, hold things in place, or separate materials — useful in many engineering designs!

exercises.question: Three designs are tested for preventing erosion. Results: Design A stops 90% of erosion, B stops 40%, C stops 70%. Which is BEST?
choices: Design B
Design C
Design A
All are equally good
exercises.exp: Design A prevents 90% of erosion — the highest percentage! More erosion prevented = better design.

exercises.question: What does it mean to ITERATE in engineering?
choices: to give up on a design
to repeat the design-test-improve cycle to make a better solution
to use the same design forever
to only build one prototype
exercises.exp: Iteration means repeating the cycle — design, test, get feedback, improve. Each cycle makes the solution better!

exercises.question: A building in a HURRICANE zone needs to withstand strong winds. Which design feature helps most?
choices: very tall thin walls
a low aerodynamic profile with a strong roof-to-wall connection
using paper as building material
having no roof
exercises.exp: Low, aerodynamic buildings with strongly connected roofs resist hurricane winds much better than tall, thin structures.

exercises.question: Engineers want to compare TWO erosion-prevention designs fairly. They must ___.
choices: test each design in completely different conditions
test both designs under the SAME conditions
guess which is better without testing
only test the cheaper one
exercises.exp: Fair testing (controlled experiments) means changing only ONE variable at a time — otherwise you cannot compare results!

exercises.question: Which material would BEST protect a building from flooding?
choices: wood
cardboard
waterproof concrete or steel
paper
exercises.exp: Waterproof concrete and steel resist water damage — wood and paper would absorb water and weaken.

exercises.question: In engineering, a PROTOTYPE is ___.
choices: the final perfect product
an early test model built to see if the design works
a drawing only
a computer simulation only
exercises.exp: A prototype is a working model built early in the design process to test ideas before making the final version.

exercises.question: What is the most important quality of a GOOD engineering solution?
choices: it is the most expensive option
it solves the identified problem effectively and safely
it is the most complex design
it uses the most materials
exercises.exp: The best engineering solution solves the problem effectively and safely — complexity and cost matter less than function!

exercises.question: What are CRITERIA in an engineering design challenge?
choices: things the design must NOT do
the specific goals and requirements that a successful solution MUST meet
the materials available for building
the tools needed for testing
exercises.exp: Criteria are the requirements for success — what the design must do. E.g., 'The bridge must hold 500 g' is a criterion. Constraints are limits (cost, time, materials).

exercises.question: What are CONSTRAINTS in an engineering design challenge?
choices: the goals a design must meet
the limits within which a design must work — budget, available materials, time, size restrictions
the best materials for the design
the step-by-step building process
exercises.exp: Constraints limit your design — you must use only these materials, spend less than $X, finish in Y time, fit in Z space. Engineers must meet criteria WITHIN constraints.

exercises.question: In an engineering design challenge, students are given: cardboard, tape, and 10 straws to build the TALLEST TOWER that can stand for 30 seconds. What are the CONSTRAINTS?
choices: the 30 seconds and tallness requirement
only cardboard, tape, and 10 straws; must stand for 30 seconds
the tower being very colourful
having more than one person building
exercises.exp: Constraints: limited materials (cardboard, tape, 10 straws) and must stand for 30 seconds. Criterion: tallest tower. The constraints limit what designs are possible!

exercises.question: Engineers often build SCALE MODELS before building the real thing. Why?
choices: scale models are more impressive to show people
scale models are cheaper and faster to build and test — allowing design problems to be found and fixed before expensive real construction begins
scale models are always more accurate than real builds
scale models replace the need for actual construction
exercises.exp: Testing a cheap small model catches design flaws early — far cheaper than discovering problems in a full-scale bridge or building. Scale models save enormous time and money!

exercises.question: What is meant by a FAIR TEST in engineering evaluation?
choices: a test where everyone agrees the design is nice
testing designs under identical conditions so that results can be compared accurately
a test where the cheapest design always wins
testing one design only
exercises.exp: Fair testing: change ONE variable at a time and keep everything else the same. If you test two erosion solutions in different soil types, you cannot compare results fairly!

exercises.question: A student tests Design A first and Design B second. Between tests, the soil dries out. The test is UNFAIR because ___.
choices: Design A got tested first — it should go second
the soil condition changed between tests — not a fair, controlled comparison
two designs cannot be tested the same day
the student should not test her own designs
exercises.exp: Changed conditions between tests mean you cannot compare results. Fair testing requires identical conditions for all designs — same soil moisture, same amount of water, same setup!

exercises.question: Engineers select MATERIALS by matching material PROPERTIES to design REQUIREMENTS. Which material best suits making a flexible water pipe?
choices: glass
rigid iron
flexible plastic (PVC) — waterproof, durable, and bendable
cardboard
exercises.exp: PVC pipe is: waterproof (won't corrode), flexible enough to bend around obstacles, strong, lightweight, and cheap. Match properties to requirements!

exercises.question: What is a CONTROLLED VARIABLE in an engineering experiment?
choices: the variable you change between tests
a variable you keep the SAME across all tests to ensure fair comparison
the result you are measuring
a variable you cannot measure
exercises.exp: Controlled variables are kept constant so only the independent variable (what you're testing) can explain any differences in results. No controlled variables = unfair test!

exercises.question: After testing three shelter designs in simulated wind, the results are: Design 1 stays standing, Design 2 partially collapses, Design 3 falls. What should the engineer do next?
choices: accept that Design 1 is perfect
analyse why Designs 2 and 3 failed, improve the weaknesses, and retest — this is the iterative design process
throw away Designs 2 and 3 completely
present Design 1 without further testing
exercises.exp: Failure is valuable! Understanding WHY Designs 2 and 3 failed tells the engineer what to fix. Iterating — improving and retesting — is how engineering solutions get better.

exercises.question: A GROUP of students gets different results testing the SAME design. What should they do?
choices: average all the results and use the mean for a more reliable conclusion
pick the result that seems best
ignore the different results
test again with only one person
exercises.exp: Multiple trials reduce the impact of random errors. Averaging results gives a more reliable answer than any single trial — repeating tests and calculating averages is standard scientific practice.

exercises.question: BIOMIMICRY is engineering inspired by nature. Velcro was inspired by burr seeds. What does biomimicry teach us?
choices: nature has no engineering lessons for humans
nature has evolved effective solutions over millions of years — engineers can use these as inspiration for innovative designs
human engineering is always better than nature
only velcro came from nature
exercises.exp: Nature has had billions of years to optimise solutions — Velcro (burrs), bullet train nose shape (kingfisher beak), swimsuits (shark skin). Biomimicry is a growing engineering field!

exercises.question: Engineers designing a SEISMICALLY safe building in an earthquake zone might ___.
choices: use the lightest, cheapest materials regardless of strength
use flexible materials and base isolation systems that absorb seismic energy rather than fighting it rigidly
make the building as tall as possible
use glass throughout for visibility
exercises.exp: Earthquake-resistant buildings use flexible steel frames (can sway without breaking), base isolators (absorb shaking at foundation), and smart shapes — engineering lessons learned from past collapses.

exercises.question: What is SUSTAINABILITY in engineering design?
choices: designing something that lasts exactly one week
designing solutions that meet current needs without depleting resources or damaging systems that future generations will need
using as many materials as possible
only using new materials, never recycled ones
exercises.exp: Sustainable engineering considers long-term impacts — using renewable materials, minimising waste and pollution, designing for longevity and repairability. Good for people AND planet.

exercises.question: A coastal community needs to protect BEACHES from erosion. Engineers propose: A) concrete sea wall, B) planted native grasses and dunes. Which is more SUSTAINABLE long-term?
choices: concrete sea wall — stronger
planted grasses and dunes — work with natural processes, self-maintain, provide habitat, and adapt over time
they are equally good
neither protects beaches
exercises.exp: Concrete walls often cause erosion elsewhere (waves deflect sideways) and decay over time. Natural dune vegetation is self-maintaining, provides wildlife habitat, and works WITH natural processes — more sustainable!

exercises.question: LOAD-BEARING TRIANGLES are used in trusses and roof structures because ___.
choices: triangles look attractive in buildings
triangles cannot be deformed — they distribute forces efficiently and are the most rigid shape. Rectangles can collapse; triangles cannot!
triangles are the cheapest shape to build
triangles trap air better
exercises.exp: A triangle is inherently rigid — push on any corner and the force distributes through all three sides. That is why bridges, towers, and roof trusses use triangles for structural strength!

exercises.question: During the DESIGN phase of engineering, what is most important?
choices: building as fast as possible
generating multiple possible solutions, sketching and planning carefully, and choosing the most promising design before building
choosing the most expensive materials
working completely alone
exercises.exp: Good planning prevents expensive mistakes. Sketching multiple ideas, considering tradeoffs, and selecting the best approach before building leads to better outcomes and less wasted material.

exercises.question: FEEDBACK from USERS improves engineering designs. Why is user feedback valuable?
choices: users always know exactly how to fix problems
users experience the design in real-world conditions and reveal problems engineers did not anticipate in the lab
feedback is only useful from expert engineers
user feedback usually makes designs worse
exercises.exp: Real-world use reveals unexpected problems — handles that hurt hands, features that confuse users, durability issues in extreme conditions. User feedback makes designs more practical and useful.

exercises.question: An engineer tests a prototype and finds it fails. She says 'This is great data!' Why is this a POSITIVE attitude toward failure?
choices: she is being dishonest about the failure
failure reveals what does NOT work — valuable information for improving the design. Every failure eliminates a bad option and points toward better ones
failure means the project should be abandoned
engineers never experience failure
exercises.exp: Thomas Edison famously said he found 1000 ways NOT to make a lightbulb. Each failure teaches you something. Engineers who embrace failure as data iterate faster to successful solutions!

exercises.question: Which engineering approach is most likely to succeed?
choices: build the first design quickly and never change it
plan carefully, build a prototype, test it, analyse results, improve the design, test again — repeating until requirements are met
copy someone else's solution exactly without testing
use only one type of material for simplicity
exercises.exp: The iterative design process — plan, build, test, improve, repeat — is the cornerstone of successful engineering. No design is perfect on the first try. Iteration leads to excellence!

exercises.question: The Engineering Design Process begins with ___.
choices: building a prototype
testing a solution
defining the problem and identifying constraints (limitations) and criteria (requirements for success)
evaluating the final design
exercises.exp: Before designing anything, engineers must clearly define: What problem are we solving? What are the constraints (cost, materials, time)? What does success look like? This is the foundation!

exercises.question: What is a PROTOTYPE?
choices: the final perfect version of a product
a working model of a design used to test and improve the design before mass production
a drawing of a future product
an old version of a product that is no longer used
exercises.exp: Prototypes are test models — not final products. Engineers build prototypes to identify problems early, test ideas, and make improvements before expensive mass production begins!

exercises.question: CRITERIA in engineering design means ___.
choices: the materials available
the budget for the project
the requirements the solution MUST meet to be considered successful
the time allowed for design
exercises.exp: Criteria define success: 'the bridge must hold 100 kg' or 'the device must cost under $50.' Without criteria, you cannot judge whether your design succeeded!

exercises.question: CONSTRAINTS in engineering design means ___.
choices: the goals the design must achieve
the limitations on a design — available materials, budget, time, size, safety requirements
the testing methods used
the final design choices made
exercises.exp: Constraints limit what engineers can do — budget limits material choices, size limits dimensions, safety codes limit certain approaches. Good engineers work creatively within constraints!

exercises.question: Why do engineers COMMUNICATE and SHARE their designs?
choices: only to impress other engineers
so others can review, critique, build on their work — collaboration and peer review improve designs and advance knowledge
sharing is required by law
it has no benefit to engineering
exercises.exp: Engineering advances through collaboration — peer review catches errors, teammates contribute ideas, and shared knowledge avoids reinventing solutions. Open communication makes engineering better!

exercises.question: What is SYSTEMS THINKING in engineering?
choices: designing only one component at a time
understanding how all parts of a system interact — changing one part can affect all others unexpectedly
using only systematic tools
thinking about only the most important part of a system
exercises.exp: Systems thinking: in complex designs, all parts interact. A car engine change affects fuel consumption, weight distribution, braking, and emissions. Engineers must think holistically!

exercises.question: TRADE-OFFS in engineering mean ___.
choices: exchanging old designs for new ones
giving up one desirable quality to gain another — e.g., lighter = less durable; cheaper = less precise
only reducing costs
design improvements always make everything better at once
exercises.exp: Every design decision involves trade-offs. Stronger metal = heavier. Faster processor = more power consumption. Engineers balance competing properties to meet their criteria.

exercises.question: REVERSE ENGINEERING means ___.
choices: designing products to work backwards
taking an existing product apart to understand how it was designed and built — learning from what already exists
destroying a prototype
returning a finished design to its starting point
exercises.exp: Reverse engineering: analyse a finished product to understand how it works. Used to learn from competitors, repair devices without manuals, and understand older technology!

exercises.question: Why do engineers use COMPUTER SIMULATIONS before building physical prototypes?
choices: to avoid all physical testing entirely
simulations are cheaper and faster — they allow testing of thousands of design variations and conditions before investing in expensive physical prototypes
computers automatically generate perfect designs
physical tests are no longer needed once computers exist
exercises.exp: CAD simulations test designs virtually — crash simulations, airflow analysis, structural stress testing — far cheaper and faster than physical testing. But physical tests are still essential for validation!

exercises.question: FAILURE ANALYSIS is an important engineering process because ___.
choices: engineers should hide failures to maintain reputation
analysing why something failed provides crucial information for improving future designs and preventing similar failures
it shows the design was useless
only successful products need analysis
exercises.exp: Failures teach more than successes! The Space Shuttle Challenger investigation revealed O-ring failures and improved safety. Post-failure analysis improves designs and saves lives.

exercises.question: What does SUSTAINABLE ENGINEERING mean?
choices: designing products that last a very long time only
engineering that meets current needs without compromising the ability of future generations to meet theirs — considering environmental, economic, and social impacts
using only natural materials
engineering that is free of cost
exercises.exp: Sustainable engineering considers the full lifecycle: raw material extraction, manufacturing, use, and disposal. Can it be recycled? Does it waste energy? What is its carbon footprint?

exercises.question: A CANTILEVER bridge extends horizontally into space, supported only at one end. Its strength comes from ___.
choices: tension cables from above
it being made of the heaviest possible material
distributing the load through balanced counterweights and the structural rigidity of the projecting beam
multiple supporting columns underneath
exercises.exp: Cantilever bridges balance: one arm of the bridge counterbalances the other. The Forth Bridge (Scotland) and Quebec Bridge use this elegant structural engineering principle!

exercises.question: BIOMEDICAL ENGINEERS apply engineering to medicine. Which is an example of their work?
choices: designing roads and bridges
designing prosthetic limbs, pacemakers, MRI machines, and drug delivery systems
analysing weather patterns
building computer networks
exercises.exp: Biomedical engineering merges medicine and engineering — prosthetics restore mobility, pacemakers regulate heartbeats, dialysis machines replace kidney function. Life-saving technology!

exercises.question: What is NANOTECHNOLOGY?
choices: technology involving very large structures
engineering at the scale of individual atoms and molecules (1-100 nanometres — 1 nm = 10⁻⁹ metres)
technology for building nano-sized houses
a type of space engineering
exercises.exp: Nanotechnology manipulates matter at atomic scale. Applications: nanoparticle drug delivery (targets cancer cells specifically), nano-coatings (waterproof clothing), carbon nanotubes (super-strong materials)!

exercises.question: ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE (AI) is becoming an engineering tool. How can AI help engineers?
choices: AI replaces all engineers completely
AI can analyse enormous datasets, optimise complex designs across millions of variables, and identify patterns humans would miss — augmenting engineering capability
AI only writes computer code
AI can only be used for art and language
exercises.exp: AI augments engineering: generative design (AI generates thousands of structural options optimised for weight/strength), failure prediction, simulating material properties. AI + human engineers = powerful combination!

exercises.question: What are the SIX SIMPLE MACHINES that all complex machines are built from?
choices: lever, pulley, wheel/axle, inclined plane, wedge, screw
lever, gear, spring, chain, magnet, motor
bolt, nut, spring, magnet, pulley, wheel
rope, ramp, wheel, hammer, nail, saw
exercises.exp: The six simple machines: lever, pulley, wheel and axle, inclined plane, wedge, and screw. All complex machines (cars, cranes, engines) are combinations of these six fundamentals!

exercises.question: Why is TESTING with a FAIR TEST so important in engineering?
choices: it makes testing faster
it ensures only ONE variable changes at a time — so you know which change caused any difference in results
it reduces the cost of testing
it replaces the need for multiple tests
exercises.exp: Fair tests: change only one variable at a time (the independent variable) while keeping all others constant. This ensures that results are caused by the change you made, not something else!

exercises.question: INFRASTRUCTURE refers to ___.
choices: the most advanced technology in a country
the fundamental engineered systems supporting society — roads, bridges, water supply, sewers, power grids, communications
only buildings and housing
only transportation systems
exercises.exp: Infrastructure is the backbone of modern society. Without reliable roads, clean water, electricity, and communications, economies and communities cannot function. Engineering maintains civilisation!

exercises.question: What is the role of QUALITY CONTROL in engineering and manufacturing?
choices: to make products look better aesthetically
to ensure every product meets the required standards and specifications — checking for defects before products reach users
to speed up production at the cost of quality
only required for medical devices
exercises.exp: Quality control: systematic checking that products meet specifications. A faulty aircraft part or medical device can be fatal. QC prevents defects reaching users — essential in all industries!
